Frequently Asked Questions:
Q: How do I install ChatCops?
A: The easiest way is via CDN: add a <script> tag with src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@chatcops/widget@1/dist/chatcops.min.js" and set data-api-url to your server endpoint. For npm: install @chatcops/widget, @chatcops/server, and optionally @chatcops/core.

Q: What is ChatCops?
A: ChatCops is an open-source, universal AI chatbot widget you can embed on any website with a single script tag. It supports Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini as AI providers.

Q: What AI providers are supported?
A: ChatCops supports Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI, and Google Gemini. You configure the provider and model on the server side — the widget is provider-agnostic.

Q: What server platforms are supported?
A: ChatCops has adapters for Express.js, Vercel Serverless/Edge Functions, and Cloudflare Workers. You can also build custom integrations using the core package.

Q: How does the lead capture tool work?
A: On the server, `new LeadCaptureTool(async (lead) => saveLead(lead))` in `tools` lets the AI collect contact details (name, email, company, project details) during the conversation and calls your function with them (Tools page). <sources>
<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/installation/" title="Installation">
Installation

ChatCops consists of three packages. Install only what you need.
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/bot/" title="ChatCopsBot" section="What it does">
ChatCopsBot > What it does

- It reads the pages listed in a sitemap, or a list of URLs it was given. It doesn't follow links to discover more.
- It obeys `robots.txt`: the `ChatCopsBot` group if there is one, otherwise `*`, including `Crawl-delay`. When `robots.txt` can't be read (a 5xx answer, or no answer), it fetches nothing from that site.
- It fetches four pages at a time by default, and sends conditional requests on later runs, so unchanged pages answer `304`.
- It keeps the readable text of each page to answer visitors' questions, with a link back to the page.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="KnowledgeSource Interface">
Knowledge Base > KnowledgeSource Interface

```typescript
import type { RetrievalQuery, RetrievedChunk } from '@chatcops/core';

interface KnowledgeSource {
  type: string;
  getContext(query: string): Promise<string>;
  // Optional: the matching chunks themselves, with the conversation so far.
  retrieve?(query: RetrievalQuery): Promise<RetrievedChunk[]>;
}
```

When a source has `retrieve`, the server uses it instead of `getContext`. It passes the visitor's message and the last few messages before it, so a follow-up like "how long does it take?" can be searched in context. The chunks from every source are numbered and given to the model in one fenced block, marked as reference material that never contains instructions, since crawled pages sometimes do. That's what citations will build on.
</source>
<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/" title="ChatCops Documentation" section="Packages">
ChatCops Documentation > Packages

| Package | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `@chatcops/widget` | Embeddable chat widget (IIFE + ESM), Shadow DOM isolated, ~7KB gzipped |
| `@chatcops/server` | Server handler + Express, Vercel, Cloudflare adapters |
| `@chatcops/core` | AI provider abstraction, tools, knowledge base, i18n, analytics |
</source>
<source id="5" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="Retrieval from a vector store">
Knowledge Base > Retrieval from a vector store

The newer Voyage models (`voyage-4`, `voyage-4-lite`, `voyage-3.5` and others) can shorten their vectors with `dimensions` (256, 512, 1024 or 2048). Other models make one fixed length, so set `dimensions` to that length. `batchSize` is how many texts go in one request (128 by default, at most 1,000); each model also limits the tokens in a request, so lower it for very long texts.

In a Cloudflare Worker, pass the `AI` binding directly:

```typescript
import {
  memoryVectors,
  retrieverKnowledge,
  vectorRetriever,
  workersAiEmbedder,
  workersAiReranker,
  type WorkersAiBinding,
} from '@chatcops/core';

declare const env: { AI: WorkersAiBinding };

const embedder = workersAiEmbedder({ ai: env.AI });
const vectors = memoryVectors({ dimensions: embedder.dimensions });
const reranker = workersAiReranker({ ai: env.AI });
const knowledge = retrieverKnowledge(vectorRetriever({ store: vectors, embedder, reranker }), { topK: 5 });
```

There are two retrievers:

| Retriever | Searches by | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `vectorRetriever({ store, embedder })` | Meaning: the question is embedded and compared with every chunk | Any vector store |
| `hybridRetriever({ store, embedder })` | Meaning and exact words, merged by rank (reciprocal rank fusion, `rrfK` 60) | A store with `keywordQuery` |

Hybrid search is the better default when the store supports it. Words catch what meaning misses, such as product names, error codes and part numbers.

Both take `candidates` (how many records each search fetches, default 20) and an optional `reranker`, which reorders the candidates before the top ones are kept. A short follow-up question ("how long does it take?") is searched together with the visitor's previous question, so it finds the right pages.
</source>

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/analytics/" title="Analytics" section="Reading Stats with Express">
Analytics > Reading Stats with Express

`chatcopsAnalyticsHandler` returns the stats for the traffic handled by `chatcopsMiddleware`. Pass the **same config object** to both so they share one handler:

```typescript
import express from 'express';
import { chatcopsMiddleware, chatcopsAnalyticsHandler } from '@chatcops/server';

const config = {
  provider: { type: 'claude', apiKey: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY! },
  systemPrompt: 'You are a helpful assistant.',
  allowedOrigins: ['*'],
  analytics: true,
  analyticsToken: process.env.CHATCOPS_ANALYTICS_TOKEN,
};

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.use('/chat', chatcopsMiddleware(config));
app.get('/analytics', chatcopsAnalyticsHandler(config));

app.listen(3001);
```

When `analyticsToken` is set, requests must include a bearer token:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:3001/analytics
```

When unset, the endpoint is public and logs a warning the first time it is hit.

With a `storage` that has an event sink (`memoryStorage()`, Postgres, Redis, SQLite and Cloudflare stores all do), the server writes every event there too, and the endpoint counts from the store. Then the stats cover every server instance, not just the one answering. Pick the range with `from` and `to` in milliseconds. The default is the last 30 days:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:3001/analytics?from=1792368000000"
```

Without a store that can be queried, the stats come from the memory of the process that answers, which on serverless is one instance at a time. A range that isn't a number gets `400 {"error":"invalid_range"}`.

`GET /analytics` responds with the aggregated stats (or `null` if `analytics` is not enabled):

```json
{
  "totalConversations": 2,
  "totalMessages": 4,
  "leadsCaptured": 0,
  "averageMessagesPerConversation": 2,
  "eventCounts": { "conversation.started": 2, "message.sent": 2, "message.received": 2 }
}
```
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/analytics/" title="Analytics" section="Storage">
Analytics > Storage

The built-in collector stores events in memory (max 1000 events). With `analytics: true` and a `storage`, the server already writes events to the store's sink, buffered and flushed as each reply ends. To do the same in your own code, use `BufferedEventSink`. It batches up to 50 events by default and flushes every 2 seconds. Call `flush()` when you need to wait for queued writes, such as before a process exits:

```typescript
import { BufferedEventSink, memoryStorage, statsFromSink } from '@chatcops/core';

const storage = memoryStorage();
const eventSink = storage.events;
if (!eventSink) throw new Error('Event storage is not configured');

const analytics = new BufferedEventSink(eventSink, {
  maxBatch: 50,
  flushMs: 2000,
});

analytics.track('pricing.viewed', { plan: 'Team' });
await analytics.flush();

const now = Date.now();
const stats = await statsFromSink(eventSink, {
  from: now - 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  to: now,
});
```

Use a persistent `EventSink` implementation when events need to be shared across processes or survive restarts. Writes that fail are logged and dropped so analytics does not interrupt chat requests. `statsFromSink` requires the sink's optional `query` method; the range includes `from` and excludes `to`. It counts each `conversation:started` event as one conversation.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/analytics/" title="Analytics" section="Enabling Analytics">

```typescript
import { chatcopsMiddleware } from '@chatcops/server';

chatcopsMiddleware({
  provider: { type: 'claude', apiKey: '...' },
  systemPrompt: '...',
  analytics: true,  // Enable analytics tracking
});
```
</source>

Knowledge Base > FAQ Knowledge Source

Best for structured question-answer pairs:

```typescript
import { FAQKnowledgeSource } from '@chatcops/core';

const faq = new FAQKnowledgeSource([

```
</source>
<source id="5" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/index-your-site/" title="Index Your Site" section="2. Check and build the index">

```bash
npx chatcops ingest --dry-run
```

If the pages look right, build the index:

```bash
npx chatcops ingest
```

Then check the search results before connecting the bot:

```bash
npx chatcops search "How do I get started?"
```

If search finds the wrong page, adjust your sources or exclude patterns in `ingest`, ingest again, and search again.

Your job is to help developers understand and use ChatCops — an open-source AI chatbot widget.

Key facts:
- ChatCops has 3 packages: @chatcops/widget (client), @chatcops/server (backend), @chatcops/core (providers/tools)
- Widget is zero-dependency, Shadow DOM isolated, and works with a single script tag
- Server supports Express, Vercel, and Cloudflare Workers
- AI providers: Claude, OpenAI, Gemini
- MIT licensed, fully open-source at github.com/codercops/chatcops

Be concise, helpful, and friendly. Use markdown formatting. If you don't know something specific, direct users to the docs.
Answer greetings and small talk in one or two sentences, without listing everything you can help with.

Frequently Asked Questions:
Q: How does the lead capture tool work?
A: On the server, `new LeadCaptureTool(async (lead) => saveLead(lead))` in `tools` lets the AI collect contact details (name, email, company, project details) during the conversation and calls your function with them (Tools page). A webhook for the `lead:captured` event posts them to a URL (Server setup page). In the browser, `ChatCops.on('leadCaptured', (lead) => { ... })` runs your code when the widget captures one (Events page).

Q: How do I install ChatCops?
A: The easiest way is via CDN: add a <script> tag with src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@chatcops/widget@1/dist/chatcops.min.js" and set data-api-url to your server endpoint. For npm: install @chatcops/widget, @chatcops/server, and optionally @chatcops/core.

Q: What server platforms are supported?
A: ChatCops has adapters for Express.js, Vercel Serverless/Edge Functions, and Cloudflare Workers. You can also build custom integrations using the core package.

Q: Does ChatCops support multiple languages?
A: The widget text is in English by default. To show it in another language, pass your translations in the widget's `strings` option. When the widget sends a `locale`, the server also asks the model to reply in that language.

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/test-before-launch/" title="Test Before Launch" section="4. Run replays in CI for free">
Test Before Launch > 4. Run replays in CI for free

When the `CI` environment variable is set (which GitHub Actions and most CI systems set automatically), `chatcops test` replays by default. You do not need to configure any API keys or secrets in your CI environment.

Add a GitHub Actions workflow at `.github/workflows/evals.yml`:

```yaml
name: Evals
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx chatcops test
```

Because `CI=true` triggers `--replay`, the entire test suite executes in milliseconds on every pull request. If a PR modifies the system prompt without updating the cassettes, CI fails, prompting the author to verify the change locally with `--record`.
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Recorded replays">
Testing your bot > Recorded replays

A few things to know about recordings:

- Headers aren't saved, and neither are query parameters like `key` or `api_key`. API keys usually travel in one of those, so they stay out of the files. The request and response bodies are saved, which means your system prompt and the replies are in the files, so treat them like the rest of your code. Request bodies stay readable JSON, so a re-recording's diff shows what you changed. Responses over 4 kB, such as a streamed reply with one event per token, are saved gzipped in base64, which keeps the files about a tenth of the size.
- `repeat` records every run, and replay plays them back in the same order.
- Replays answer at once, so `latency` in a replayed run is not the real latency.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Recorded replays">
Testing your bot > Recorded replays

Running tests calls your model for real, which costs tokens and needs the API key. For CI, record the calls once and replay them:

```bash
npx chatcops test --record   # calls the APIs and saves what they answer
npx chatcops test --replay   # answers every call from the recordings
```

`--record` saves each eval file's calls next to it, in `__cassettes__/<file>.jsonl` (so `evals/pricing.chat.yaml` records to `evals/__cassettes__/pricing.chat.jsonl`). It records every HTTP call a test makes: the model, embedding calls for knowledge search, and tools that call APIs without a mock. Commit the folder with your eval files.

When the `CI` environment variable is set, as it is on GitHub Actions and most CI services, `chatcops test` replays by default, so CI needs no API keys and costs nothing. A provider config without an `apiKey` gets a stand-in key during replay, since nothing is sent. Keep the config file loading when a key is missing: read `process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as it is, and don't throw at load time. `--live` calls the APIs anyway.

Each call is matched by its method, URL and body within its test. Any change that changes what gets sent fails the test instead of passing on an old answer:

- a new word in the system prompt
- another model
- a tool added or removed
- a new knowledge page in the context

The message says where the request changed:

```text
✗ evals/pricing.chat.yaml > quotes the Team price
    A call changed since it was recorded (POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages, at system[0].text). Run chatcops test --record to record it again.
```

Run `--record` again after a change like that, check that the tests still pass, and commit the new recordings. `--record --filter` updates only the tests it ran, and recordings of tests you deleted are dropped the next time the file is recorded.

A few things to know about recordings:
</source>
<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Recorded replays > JUnit reports for CI">
Testing your bot > Recorded replays > JUnit reports for CI

Write a JUnit report for a CI test report integration:

```bash
npx chatcops test --reporter junit --output evals.xml
```

To keep the readable summary in the terminal and save XML separately, give the JUnit reporter a destination:

```bash
npx chatcops test --reporter pretty --reporter junit=evals.xml
```

File paths are relative to the current folder. Parent folders are created as needed, and an existing report is replaced after reporting finishes. Paths containing `=` work: only the first `=` separates the reporter name from its destination. Each reporter name can be used once, and file destinations must differ. `--output` is a shortcut for one reporter; it cannot be combined with multiple reporters or `name=file`. A file write error exits 2, after all reporters have finished and any recordings have been saved.

JUnit groups tests by eval file. Each test's time is the sum of its turns' latencies across all repeats, in seconds. The aggregate pass-rate verdict decides whether the testcase passed. A failed test with any execution error gets an `<error>`; other failed tests get a `<failure>` with the assertion reasons, turn numbers and replies.

For example, GitLab CI can display the report even when an eval fails (record the API calls first so CI can replay them):

```yaml
evals:
  image: node:22
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx chatcops test --reporter junit --output evals.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: evals.xml
```
</source>
<source id="5" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/test-before-launch/" title="Test Before Launch" section="3. Record calls into cassettes > Why replays are deterministic and free">
Test Before Launch > 3. Record calls into cassettes > Why replays are deterministic and free

Run the suite with `--replay`:

```bash
npx chatcops test --replay
```

Instead of sending requests over the Internet, `--replay` matches each call by its HTTP method, URL, and request body within the test, returning the recorded response immediately.

Replays offer two critical benefits:

1. **Zero cost and zero keys**: Replaying makes no outbound network requests. It spends zero tokens and requires no provider API keys.
2. **Strict regression detection**: If someone changes a word in the system prompt, swaps the model, or alters tool schemas, the request hash changes. Rather than silently passing with stale data, the test immediately flags the mismatch:

```text
✗ evals/launch.chat.yaml > quotes Starter and Pro plan pricing
    A call changed since it was recorded (POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages, at system[0].text). Run chatcops test --record to record it again.
```

Commit `evals/__cassettes__/` to Git alongside your YAML eval files. Whenever you intentionally change your prompt or configuration, re-record with `npx chatcops test --record` and commit the updated cassette.

Sensitive values like `Authorization` headers, Bearer tokens, and `?key=` query parameters are never stored in cassettes, keeping your secrets safe.
</source>
</sources>

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Eval files">
Testing your bot > Eval files

By default the command runs every `evals/**/*.chat.yaml` file. Pass globs to pick others:

```bash
npx chatcops test "evals/pricing/*.chat.yaml"
```

An eval file has a name and a list of tests. Each test is one conversation, a turn at a time:

```yaml
version: 1
name: Pricing
tests:
  - name: quotes the Team price
    tags: [pricing]
    turns:
      - user: How much is the Team plan?
        expect:
          - contains: "$19"
          - not-contains: "$29"

  - name: remembers the plan on a follow-up
    turns:
      - user: Tell me about the Team plan.
      - user: How much is it per year?
        expect:
          - contains: "$190"
```

Each assertion has one key. `judge` has a model grade the reply ([below](#judged-by-a-model)), and every assertion also works with a `not-` prefix to say the opposite. An assertion name that doesn't exist fails the whole run before anything is sent, so a typo can't make a test pass by checking nothing.

Four assertions check what the reply says:

- `contains`: takes a string or a list of strings that must all appear in the reply (`contains: "$19"` or `contains: [Team, "$19"]`).
- `icontains`: case-insensitive substring matching; takes a string or a list of strings (`icontains: team` or `icontains: [team, "$19"]`).
- `regex`: matches the reply against a JavaScript `RegExp`. Accepts a pattern string (`regex: "\\$\\d+"`) or `{ pattern, flags }` (`regex: { pattern: "team", flags: "i" }`).
- `equals`: compares the trimmed reply with the exact expected string (`equals: "The Team plan is $19."`).

Three assertions catch a prompt change that makes replies longer, slower or more expensive:
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Judged by a model">
Testing your bot > Judged by a model

Some things a reply should do don't fit in a `contains`: "confirms the demo without inventing a meeting time", "apologizes once and doesn't argue". A `judge` assertion has a second model grade the reply against a rubric:

```yaml
expect:
  - judge: "Confirms the demo request without inventing a meeting time."
  - judge: { rubric: "Apologizes once and doesn't argue.", threshold: 0.8 }
```

The judge sees the rubric and the conversation so far, scores the last reply from 0 to 1, and gives a reason. The assertion passes at `threshold` or above (0.7 when you don't set one), and a failure prints the score and the reason.

By default the judge is the cheap model of a different provider than your bot's: Gemini's default model, or OpenAI's when the bot runs on Gemini. A model grading its own answers tends to score them too kindly. Its key comes from `GEMINI_API_KEY` (or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`), `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and without one the run stops before it starts instead of skipping the judged tests. Every run prints which judge it used. To choose it yourself, pass `--judge-model openai:gpt-5-mini`, or set `judge` in the config:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@chatcops/cli';

export default defineConfig({
  server: { provider: { type: 'claude', apiKey: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY! }, systemPrompt: 'You answer questions about Acme.' },
  judge: { type: 'openai', apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY!, model: 'gpt-5-mini' },
});
```

A judge's scores can change when its model changes, so keep the same judge for a suite, and re-record when you switch. Judge calls are recorded and replayed like the bot's, so in CI the same verdicts come back without a key.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/test-before-launch/" title="Test Before Launch" section="1. Write your first eval file">
Test Before Launch > 1. Write your first eval file

By default, `chatcops test` looks for any `evals/**/*.chat.yaml` file. Create a file at `evals/launch.chat.yaml`.

```yaml
version: 1
name: Pre-launch Bot Verification
tests:
  - name: quotes Starter and Pro plan pricing
    tags: [pricing]
    turns:
      - user: How much do your plans cost?
        expect:
          - contains: ["Starter", "$29", "Pro", "$79"]

  - name: captures a sales lead
    tags: [leads]
    turns:
      - user: I would like an enterprise demo. My name is Alex, email is alex@example.com, and we need SSO with 50 seats.
        expect:
          - calls-tool: capture_lead
          - lead-captured: true

  - name: politely declines off-topic requests
    tags: [guardrails]
    turns:
      - user: Can you write me a poem about the ocean?
        expect:
          - judge: "Politely declines and steers the visitor back to Acme's products."
```

- **Tone and brevity**: Verifying greetings remain concise and helpful without unsolicited essays or repetitive apologies.
- **Knowledge retrieval and citations**: Confirming questions about your documentation cite the right URLs using the `cites` assertion.
- **Admitting unknown information**: Ensuring the bot clearly says it doesn't know when a question isn't answered in your documentation, rather than hallucinating.

```typescript
import type { JSONSchema, MessagePart, ToolParameter } from '@chatcops/core';

  parameters?: Record<string, ToolParameter>;   // the older flat form
```

Upgrading from 0.5

This release changes a lot inside the server: how replies are run and stored, how limits are counted, and what goes over the wire. Most apps upgrade without code changes, because old widgets keep working against the new server and the new widget keeps working against an old server. This page lists what can need your attention, then the new options worth turning on.

Upgrading to 1.0

1.0 removes the options and methods that 0.6 to 0.8 marked as deprecated. Each one now fails at startup with a message that names what to use instead and links here, so an upgrade can't quietly change how your chat behaves. After 1.0, ChatCops follows semver strictly: a breaking change waits for 2.0.

The one thing 1.0 keeps from 0.x on purpose is the 0.5 stream format. A widget older than 0.6, or a client that doesn't send `"protocol": 1`, still gets it, so pages with an old widget cached or pinned on a CDN keep working. It, and `regenerate: true` in requests (what those widgets send), go away in 2.0. The server logs `legacy_stream_format` the first time it answers in it, so you can tell when it's safe to stop caring.

<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/server/setup/" title="Server Setup" section="Budgets">
Server Setup > Budgets

Budgets cap what replies can cost, so a script hammering your endpoint can't run up the bill. They're counted in `storage`, so they hold across instances.

They're on by default:

| Scope | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `perConversation` | 200 replies | The widget keeps a conversation across visits, so this counts replies rather than tokens, which would grow with the size of your system prompt. |
| `perIpPerDay` | 2M tokens | The cost backstop. A script can start new conversations at will, but not new IPs as easily. |
| `globalPerDay` | none | No single number fits every site. Set one. |

The server logs the budgets in force once at startup:

```
[chatcops] Budgets: 200 replies per conversation (default), 2M tokens per IP per day (default). No daily total is set; `budgets.globalPerDay` caps your whole bill. Set `budgets` to change them, or `budgets: false` to turn them off.
```

A scope you set replaces its default whole. `false` turns a scope off, and `budgets: false` turns them all off:

```typescript
import type { ChatCopsServerConfig } from '@chatcops/server';

const config: Partial<ChatCopsServerConfig> = {
  budgets: {
    perConversation: { tokens: 400_000 },            // over the conversation's lifetime
    perIpPerDay: { tokens: 2_000_000, messages: 200 },
    globalPerDay: { usd: 20 },                        // the backstop
    // What a request cost, for the dollar cap. Price cached input at its discount.
    price: (usage: { inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number }) => (usage.inputTokens * 1 + usage.outputTokens * 5) / 1_000_000,
  },
};
```
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/server/setup/" title="Server Setup" section="Budgets">
Server Setup > Budgets

Tokens count input and output at face value, and every request sends the conversation so far, so a long conversation uses up a token budget faster than its length suggests. Budgets are checked before each model request and charged after it, so a reply can go over by one request, and each request asks for no more output than is left. A used-up budget ends the reply with an error instead of calling the model, and the server logs which one.

The per-IP budget needs the visitor's IP, so it's skipped for requests where the adapter can't tell.

For persistent conversations, custom stores, Postgres, Redis, and the storage capabilities available to the server, see [the storage page](/server/storage/).
</source>

```
[chatcops] ERROR: Allowed origin "acme.com" must start with http:// or https://.
[chatcops] Security: chat allowed from acme.com; session tokens on (900s); Turnstile off.
```

Then go through the list:

- `allowedOrigins` lists your sites, and nothing else. `['*']` is the default.
- `storage` is a store package, so limits and budgets hold across instances.
- `budgets.globalPerDay` is set to a number you're fine paying on a bad day.
- `sessionSecrets` is set, from a secret store, never a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or `VITE_` variable. Set `allowAnonymous: true` with it if widgets before 0.6 are still cached on your pages, and drop it after a few days.
- On a host other than Vercel, Cloudflare or Express, `clientIp` reads your platform's header. Otherwise per-IP limits are skipped.
- If you use the analytics endpoint, `analyticsToken` is set. Without it the endpoint is public.
- Each tool checks its own input. The model writes it, and a visitor can steer the model, so treat a tool's input like a form submission: check ids belong to the visitor, and keep write actions behind your own auth.

<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/server/setup/" title="Server Setup" section="Session tokens">

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/api/" title="API Reference" section="Methods > `ChatCops.setUser(user)`">
API Reference > Methods > `ChatCops.setUser(user)`

Tell the widget who the signed-in visitor is.

- `token` is the identity token for [signed-in visitors](/server/setup/#signed-in-visitors), which your server signs. It can also be a function (sync or async) that returns a fresh token each time the widget asks for a session, the same as [`userToken`](/server/setup/#a-fresh-token-for-each-session).
- `name` and `email` are sent to the bot as visitor details with the first message of a conversation, and the name greets them.

Switching to another user, or `setUser(null)` when the visitor signs out, clears the chat, so one person's conversation never shows for the next. With a function, passing the same function again counts as the same visitor and keeps the chat; a different function, a string or no token counts as another visitor and clears it. Keep one reference to the function if you call `setUser` more than once. With the script tag build, a call before the chat has loaded is kept until it does.

```typescript
declare const session: { name: string; email: string; chatToken: string };

ChatCops.setUser({ name: session.name, email: session.email, token: session.chatToken });

// Or, so the token is signed when the chat needs it and cannot have expired:
const signToken = async () => (await fetch('/api/chat-token')).text();
ChatCops.setUser({ name: session.name, email: session.email, token: signToken });

// When the visitor signs out:
ChatCops.setUser(null);
```

`setUser` replaces the identity the widget was started with, including a [`userToken` function](/server/setup/#a-fresh-token-for-each-session).
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/server/setup/" title="Server Setup" section="Session tokens > Signed-in visitors">
Server Setup > Session tokens > Signed-in visitors

When your site knows who the visitor is, it can tell the chat. Your server signs a short `userToken` for the signed-in user, and the widget sends it when it asks for a session:

```typescript
import type { ChatCopsServerConfig } from '@chatcops/server';

const config: Partial<ChatCopsServerConfig> = {
  identity: {
    secret: process.env.CHATCOPS_IDENTITY_SECRET!,   // at least 32 bytes, shared with your site's server
    tiers: { pro: { perConversation: { messages: 1000 } } },
  },
};
```

The token is an HS256 JWT with `sub` (the user id, up to 128 characters), `exp` in seconds, and optionally `tier`. Sign it on your server, never in the browser. With Node.js and no library:

```typescript
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto';

function chatUserToken(userId: string, tier?: string): string {
  const encode = (value: object) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(value)).toString('base64url');
  const body = `${encode({ alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' })}.${encode({ sub: userId, exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 86_400, tier })}`;
  return `${body}.${createHmac('sha256', process.env.CHATCOPS_IDENTITY_SECRET!).update(body).digest('base64url')}`;
}
```

Then put it on the page with `data-user-token="..."` on the script tag, or `userToken` in `ChatCops.init()`.

The user id goes into the session token and is stored on the conversation with its first message. The same user can resume that conversation later with a fresh token, even without the old session token. Another user, or an anonymous visitor, can't. A `tier` swaps in that tier's budgets (merged over `budgets`) for the user's replies. A `userToken` that doesn't verify or has expired gets `401 session_required`, rather than an anonymous session, so a bug on your site shows up. The widget sends the token every time it asks for a session, so give it a lifetime longer than a visit, such as a day.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/getting-started/upgrading/" title="Upgrading from 0.5" section="Things to check > One reply per conversation at a time">

<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/server/security/" title="Security" section="Always on">
Security > Always on

These need no config:

- Visitor-supplied text (the page URL and title, pre-chat answers) goes into a separate block marked as untrusted data, never into your system prompt. It's capped at 4,000 characters.
- Pre-chat answers are stored with the first message and can't be changed later in the conversation. `preChatFields` drops any field you didn't ask for.
- Request bodies over 256 KB get `413`, and every field has a length cap.
- Tool definitions are checked when the server starts, and a tool call whose arguments aren't valid JSON gets an error result instead of running.

Pre-chat Form

The pre-chat form collects information such as a visitor's name, email, or reason for contacting you before the conversation begins. Configure it in JavaScript with `ChatCops.init()`:

```typescript
import ChatCops from '@chatcops/widget';

ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.com/chat',
  preChatForm: {
    enabled: true,
    title: 'Before we start...',
    subtitle: 'Tell us a bit about yourself',
    submitLabel: 'Start chat',
    fields: [
      { name: 'name', type: 'text', label: 'Name', placeholder: 'Your name', required: true },
      { name: 'email', type: 'email', label: 'Email', placeholder: 'you@example.com' },
      {
        name: 'topic',
        type: 'select',
        label: 'What can we help with?',
        options: ['Sales', 'Support', 'Billing'],
      },
      { name: 'message', type: 'textarea', label: 'Message', placeholder: 'How can we help?' },
    ],
  },
  onPreChatSubmit(data) {
    console.log('Pre-chat answers:', data);
  },
});
```

The form appears when there is no saved conversation with messages and the visitor has not already submitted the form for the saved conversation. The answers are kept with the conversation, so they last as long as it does (see [saved conversations](/widget/configuration/#saved-conversations)). After submission, the widget switches to the chat view. If a field is named `name`, its answer personalizes the welcome message. If a field is named `message`, its answer is sent as the conversation's first chat message immediately after submission.
</source>

| Option | Type | Description |

| `name` | `string` | Required key for the answer. Use `name` to personalize the welcome message or `message` to start the chat with the visitor's answer. |
| `type` | `'text' \| 'email' \| 'select' \| 'textarea'` | Required input type. Email fields are checked for a valid email format. |
| `label` | `string` | Required text label displayed above the field. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | Optional placeholder. For a select, this replaces the default prompt. If omitted, the select prompt comes from `strings.selectPlaceholder` (English default: `Select {label}...`). |
| `required` | `boolean` | Optional. When `true`, submitting with an empty value shows an error and focuses the field. Defaults to `false`. |
| `options` | `string[]` | Optional choices for a `select` field. |

On submit, required fields are checked for non-empty values, and non-empty `email` fields are checked for email format. Invalid fields show an error, focus moves to the first invalid field, and the form stays open until corrected. Values are trimmed before they are submitted.

Tell the widget who the signed-in visitor is.

- `token` is the identity token for [signed-in visitors](/server/setup/#signed-in-visitors), which your server signs. It can also be a function (sync or async) that returns a fresh token each time the widget asks for a session, the same as [`userToken`](/server/setup/#a-fresh-token-for-each-session).
- `name` and `email` are sent to the bot as visitor details with the first message of a conversation, and the name greets them.

Switching to another user, or `setUser(null)` when the visitor signs out, clears the chat, so one person's conversation never shows for the next. With a function, passing the same function again counts as the same visitor and keeps the chat; a different function, a string or no token counts as another visitor and clears it. Keep one reference to the function if you call `setUser` more than once. With the script tag build, a call before the chat has loaded is kept until it does.

```typescript

ChatCops.setUser({ name: session.name, email: session.email, token: session.chatToken });

// Or, so the token is signed when the chat needs it and cannot have expired:
const signToken = async () => (await fetch('/api/chat-token')).text();
ChatCops.setUser({ name: session.name, email: session.email, token: signToken });

// When the visitor signs out:
ChatCops.setUser(null);
```

```typescript
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.com/chat',
  preChatForm: { enabled: true, fields: [{ name: 'email', type: 'email', label: 'Email' }] },
  onPreChatSubmit(data) {
    analytics.track('pre_chat_submitted', data);
  },
});
```

The widget also emits a `preChatSubmit` event with the same `Record<string, string>` payload. Subscribe with [`ChatCops.on()`](/widget/events#prechatsubmit):

```typescript
ChatCops.on('preChatSubmit', (data) => {
  console.log('Pre-chat form submitted:', data);
});
```

Pre-chat forms can only be configured through JavaScript. There are no `data-*` attributes for `preChatForm` or its callbacks.

Frequently Asked Questions:
Q: Does ChatCops support multiple languages?
A: The widget text is in English by default. To show it in another language, pass your translations in the widget's `strings` option. When the widget sends a `locale`, the server also asks the model to reply in that language.

Q: How does the lead capture tool work?
A: On the server, `new LeadCaptureTool(async (lead) => saveLead(lead))` in `tools` lets the AI collect contact details (name, email, company, project details) during the conversation and calls your function with them (Tools page). A webhook for the `lead:captured` event posts them to a URL (Server setup page). In the browser, `ChatCops.on('leadCaptured', (lead) => { ... })` runs your code when the widget captures one (Events page).

Q: Can I customize the widget appearance?
A: The widget uses a dark theme by default. You can customize the accent color, text and background colors, font, border radius, and position through the theme configuration.

Q: What AI providers are supported?
A: ChatCops supports Claude (Anthropic), OpenAI, and Google Gemini. You configure the provider and model on the server side — the widget is provider-agnostic.

Q: How do I install ChatCops?
A: The easiest way is via CDN: add a <script> tag with src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@chatcops/widget@1/dist/chatcops.min.js" and set data-api-url to your server endpoint. For npm: install @chatcops/widget, @chatcops/server, and optionally @chatcops/core.

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/theming/" title="Theming" section="CSS tokens > Upgrading from a dark-only version">
Theming > CSS tokens > Upgrading from a dark-only version

Earlier versions of the widget were always dark. Now it's light on light systems, which suits most sites better. To keep the old look everywhere, set `mode: 'dark'` (or `data-theme-mode="dark"`).

If your config sets `bgColor` or `textColor` and no `mode`, the widget picks the mode those colors were made for: a dark `bgColor` or a light `textColor` means dark, so a custom dark theme keeps working as it was.
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/theming/" title="Theming" section="Light, dark and auto">
Theming > Light, dark and auto

The widget has a light and a dark look. By default (`mode: 'auto'`) it follows the visitor's system setting, and switches while the page is open when that setting changes. Pin one with `mode`:

```typescript
ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: '/api/chat',
  theme: {
    mode: 'light',               // 'light', 'dark' or 'auto' (the default)
    accent: '#4f46e5',           // buttons, the launcher, visitor messages
    accentDark: '#a5b4fc',       // the accent in dark mode; defaults to accent
    fontFamily: 'Inter, sans-serif',
    borderRadius: 12,            // px if a number, or any CSS length like '1rem'
    tokens: {
      border: '#d0d4da',
      'panel-width': '440px',
    },
    position: 'bottom-right',    // or 'bottom-left'
  },
});
```

On the script tag, these are `data-theme-mode`, `data-accent` and `data-accent-dark`.

| Element | Light | Dark |
|---------|-------|------|
| Background | `#ffffff` | `#0a0a0a` |
| Surface (bot messages, header) | `#f4f5f7` | `#1a1a1a` |
| Input area | `#ffffff` | `#2a2a2a` |
| Border | `#d9dce1` | `#333333` |
| Text | `#1a1d23` | `#ffffff` |
| Secondary text | `#5b616e` | `#a0a0a0` |
| Accent | `#4f46e5` | `#6366f1` |
| Errors | `#c62828` | `#ef4444` |

The dark look is the one the widget had before light mode existed. Text on the accent is picked for contrast (white or near-black, with the accent darkened a little when neither reaches 4.5:1), in each mode for its own accent.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/theming/" title="Theming" section="CSS Override (Advanced)">
Theming > CSS Override (Advanced)

You can override widget styles by targeting the host element. The first widget on a page has the id `chatcops-root`, and every widget host has the class `chatcops-root`, so use `.chatcops-root` to style all of them. For a CSS-only override in one pinned mode, target its `data-cc-mode` value:

```css
.chatcops-root[data-cc-mode="dark"] {
  --cc-border: #d0d4da;
  --cc-panel-width: 440px;
}
```

The host has `data-cc-mode="light"` or `"dark"` when that mode is selected explicitly.
</source>
<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/theming/" title="Theming" section="ThemeConfig Interface">
Theming > ThemeConfig Interface

```typescript
import type { WidgetTokens } from '@chatcops/widget';

interface ThemeConfig {
  mode?: 'light' | 'dark' | 'auto';  // Default 'auto': follows the system setting
  accent?: string;          // Hex color
  accentDark?: string;      // Hex color, the accent in dark mode. Defaults to accent
  textColor?: string;       // Hex color
  bgColor?: string;         // Hex color
  fontFamily?: string;      // CSS font-family string
  borderRadius?: string | number;  // px if a number or numeric string (12, '12'), or any CSS length ('1rem')
  tokens?: WidgetTokens;    // Partial CSS tokens, named without the '--cc-' prefix; applied in every mode
  position?: 'bottom-right' | 'bottom-left';
}
```
